A brand new documentary titled "All of Us" has landed on Apple TV, telling the story of a public primary school that takes a unique approach to caring for students with diverse needs, opening up new possibilities for education.

Both iPhone and iPad play an important role in this story, and have been described as a powerful example of how inclusive education can benefit every child...

Traditionally, students with special needs, whether due to disabilities or other reasons, have often been separated from mainstream students for lessons. The conventional thinking has been that putting everyone in the same classroom could be disruptive for the majority of students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary chose a different path, and the results have proven that inclusive teaching not only does not cause disruption, but actually benefits the academic and social development of all students. The results have been so remarkable that the school's principal and a kindergarten teacher were both named Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year respectively in 2025.

This 70-minute documentary is now streaming on Apple TV, telling the story of a "school that breaks the mold."

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn together in regular classrooms. Every child does maths together, reads together, and sings together in music lessons. Teachers and various specialists work closely together in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves. How do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school, with no extra funding, no additional staff, and no magic tricks. It's simply a group of educators who decided to stop separating their students and chose to believe in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mold, a school that is unique but really shouldn't have to be unique.

iPad and iPhone play an important role

Some students have severe communication difficulties, and Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) apps running on iPad and iPhone have dramatically improved their ability to interact with teachers and fellow students.

One important finding is that AAC apps are not just helpful for students with communication difficulties — they are equally useful for all students. Founding principal Cathi Davis told me:

Whether it's students with higher reading and language abilities, or those just beginning to build communication or language skills, when they can use them to generate, expand, or express ideas through AAC tools, they show extremely high levels of engagement. We can rely on this always-available communication support to overcome issues like limited writing stamina, or even eliminate the stress of projecting ideas loudly, while breaking down the various barriers that frequently appear in the classroom and in life... This is truly the best embodiment of what we call 'universal design' — more than any other language, communication, or vocabulary tool in the classroom, it is truly a tool that belongs to everyone.

The facts revealed in the documentary prove that this teaching approach works for all students, not just those with special needs — this point is indisputable. The documentary's dedicated website also offers a comprehensive series of video resources, in the hope that other schools can learn from the Ruby Bridges experience.
